newsitem.title: INDIA: Pre-budget buying seen driving Indian shares.
newsitem.headline: Pre-budget buying seen driving Indian shares.

text.p: Volatile Indian stock markets are expected to repeat their traditional pre-budget rally this week, brokers and analysts said.
"I expect the market to be buoyant but choppy at times," said Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) member-broker Ramesh Damani. "This is a liquidity-driven rally."
He said foreign and domestic funds were pumping cash into selective blue-chip stocks because these were good bargains compared to other emerging markets.
"India has been the best performing stock market this year in the Asian equity universe," Christopher Wood at Peregrine Capital said in a recent report. "The market should continue to perform."
India's Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is scheduled to unveil the federal budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) on February 28.
Analysts said expectations of incentives for industry to boost investments in infrastructure ventures like power, roads and ports, where chronic shortages have undermined India's growth, were high.
"There'll be sops for industry," said Kush Katakia, a dealer at broker V.C. Mehta. "We'll see measures to lure foreign investors into core sectors."
He said talk of increases in railway freight and oil prices, both heavily subsidised by the government, were already discounted by the market.
"People know this is inevitable," Katakia said. "I don't think anyone will be surprised."
Other analysts said the government was unlikely to raise oil prices steeply.
"Increase in petrol and fuel prices are unlikely to be sharp and may be phased," said G.P. Gupta, chairman of Unit Trust of India (UTI), the country's biggest mutual fund.
Brokers said news that the UTI was likely to be a net buyer was sufficient reason for the market to be upbeat.
One of the strongest factors given for the sharp fall in share prices during calendar 1996 was UTI's heavy selling to meet its huge redemption commitments.
The BSE index hit a three-year low of 2,713.12 on December 4, 1996.
Analysts expect Chidambaram to restore certain tax exemptions for investments in UTI units, which would boost its mobilisation of funds and investments in stock markets.
But doubts of the 13-party coalition government's capability to push through reforms remain.
"India still depends on the government making a modicum of moves, in terms of deregulation and macro-economic policy, to unleash the economy's obvious growth potential," Peregrine's Wood said.
"The present coalition government continues to lack the political will to push through a sweeping reform agenda."
Despite these apprehensions the benchmark BSE's top-30 index was likely to test 3,750 or 3,800 before the budget, broker Damani said.
Last week the index jumped 114.77 points, or 3.37 percent, to 3,521.99.
"Left to me I'm not hopeful on the budget. The government hasn't much to give to satisfy expectations," he said. "But, the market will still rally (ahead of the budget)."
